abstract.text: The transparent view over the video that takes keyboard, mouse, and touch input for the Mac.

inlineContent.text: It is the first responder while input is active, so hardware key presses arrive here and are
not passed up the responder chain. iPadOS still handles some shortcuts before any app sees
them: Cmd-Tab, Cmd-H, Cmd-Space, Cmd-Shift-3/4/5, the Globe key and its combinations, and
Control-arrows when Stage Manager is on. Those never reach the Mac.

abstract.text: Presses the buttons of trackpad and mouse clicks that UIKit delivers as pointer touches.
Hands one touch step to the router’s queue, unless a three- or four-finger stroke is silent.
Whether three fingers drag, with the swipes on four fingers, as macOS’s own setting does.
One change to the on-screen keyboard’s text, as the Mac must see it: backspaces, then new text.
Which hardware keys go to the Mac while the on-screen keyboard’s text view is first responder.
A pinch on the glass or the trackpad, as zoom steps.
Taps, a long press, a one-finger drag, a three-finger drag, a pinch, three kinds of scroll,
and the stroke observer for three- and four-finger gestures.
Feeds GameController mouse motion and buttons into the router while enabled.
Hovers the Pencil over the picture, on the iPads that sense it in the air.
Feeds every finger to the stroke observer, which hands its gestures to the router.
The buttons in a pointer event’s mask, taking an empty mask as a primary click.
Whether the on-screen keyboard is up for typing to the Mac.
Turns hardware key presses into key-down and key-up events, each key down at most once.
What a pinch recogniser’s state asks of the router.
An invisible text view that takes the on-screen keyboard and dictation, and reports each edit.
Adds the invisible text view that takes the on-screen keyboard and dictation while it is up.
Whether input should flow to the Mac: streaming with no sheet up.
Puts the input surface over the video, handing it the mode and the Mac’s content rect the reducer owns.
Says which characters Bluetooth couldn’t type, because the Mac’s keyboard layout has no keys for them.
The transparent view over the video that takes keyboard, mouse, and touch input for the Mac.
Turns three-finger drag on or off; on, the swipes take four fingers, as on a Mac.
The iPad and iPhone app: one screen that shows the Mac’s picture and sends the Mac input from touch, trackpad, mouse, Pencil, and keyboard.
Routes the Pencil’s touches as pen samples: where it is, how hard it presses, how it leans.
The one place every input router delivers to: the active input sink, and the switch between sinks.
Takes or gives up focus; giving it up releases everything held, first responder or not.
Merges button presses that reach the app twice into one press per click.
The input hot path: takes keyboard, mouse, and touch input and emits input events in arrival order.
A silent three- or four-finger stroke holds back a pinch’s steps, never its end, so the
next pinch still starts at its own scale.
Called when the person hides the on-screen keyboard.
Turns touch gestures into input events for the pointer mode in effect.
A glass row of the keys iPadOS won’t pass to the app: back and forward, Mission Control, Apps, brightness and media.
Follows focus, and lets go of a held drag when the surface leaves the window.
How the app’s reducers fit together, and how a touch or a key press reaches the Mac without passing through them.
Called once when a finger or pencil touches down, to wake the settings button.
